videos.title: How does an observation become a hypothesis an experiment can test, and why should new evidence change it?
videos.mainLearnerQuestion: How does an observation become a hypothesis an experiment can test, and why should new evidence change it?
videos.onScreenHeading: How does a question become a hypothesis you can test?

syllabusActions.text: Use observations and scientific knowledge and understanding to propose questions and hypotheses for scientific investigations involving primary and secondary data
Evaluate questions and hypotheses based on scientific knowledge
Modify questions and hypotheses to reflect new evidence

entryKnowledge.idea: Enzymes speed reactions at an active site; temperature changes collision rate and, above the optimum, the active site's shape; enzyme graphs rise, peak and fall.
Photosynthesis needs light and carbon dioxide (attempt context only).
Fair tests, a prediction, a table of results.

videos.biologyContext: Potato catalase foaming in hydrogen peroxide at different temperatures (the apparatus already on fa1-v20's final frame); attempts on pondweed in light.
videos.openingFrame: Open on bio-y11-fa1-v20's final frame (its Next chip edited to this video's on-screen heading).
videos.startBoundary: Recall the preceding result in one sentence, then start from the main learner question with a concrete biology observation.
videos.stopBoundary: Observation to scientific question; hypothesis in the if, then, because form with a biological reason; primary and secondary data as two ways to answer; four checks for questions and hypotheses (testable, specific, reasoned, could be shown wrong); new evidence (falling rate above the optimum) modifies the question and hypothesis. Not taught: planning the test (fa1-v21), controls, repeats, risk.

videos.title: Why must a biology plan justify its variables and controls, its sources, its risks and its ethics before any data are collected?
videos.mainLearnerQuestion: Why must a biology plan justify its variables and controls, its sources, its risks and its ethics before any data are collected?
videos.onScreenHeading: What makes a biology plan valid, reliable and ethical?

syllabusActions.text: Justify the use of independent, dependent and controlled variables, and experimental controls in a valid scientific investigation
Explain how reliable primary data is obtained
Assess the reliability of secondary data and information when planning
Assess potential hazards and their associated risks to develop a risk assessment
Select appropriate materials and technologies to design a scientific investigation
Discuss ethical issues in the development and use of scientific knowledge

videos.sourceLessonNote: No Working scientifically lesson exists on the site (teaching-app-fix biology/year11 has fa1, fa2 and fa3 only; checked 23 Nov 2026). Contexts come from the Year 11 Biology designs named in entryKnowledge.

placement.rule: Restore-and-pass: the WS video opens on its predecessor's final frame and ends on that same frame (the successor's opening frame), so only the predecessor's Next chip text changes. See bio-y11-gap-fix-status-2026-11-23.md, change C5.

entryKnowledge.idea: Change / Measure / Keep the same; independent, dependent and controlled variables; the boiled-disc control; three trials and a mean; validity, reliability; a three-row risk assessment.
Surface-area-to-volume ratio and the rate of exchange.

videos.biologyContext: Planning a potato-cylinder osmosis investigation (salt solutions; content from fa1-v09 to v11), so the agar plan stays fa2-v03's; secondary-source reliability with two claims about osmosis; ethics with a classmates' heart-rate plan and the 3Rs for animal work.
videos.openingFrame: Open on bio-y11-fa2-v02's final frame (its Next chip edited to this video's on-screen heading).
videos.startBoundary: Recall the preceding result in one sentence, then start from the main learner question with a concrete biology observation.
videos.stopBoundary: Justify, not just name: why each controlled variable would itself change the result, and what an experimental control rules out (distinct from a controlled variable); repeats and suitable equipment for reliable primary data; assessing secondary sources (who, how, when, why, agreement); hazard, likelihood, consequence and control; choosing materials and technologies for the measurement; ethical issues in developing and using knowledge (animals: replace, reduce, refine; people: consent, privacy, fair use of results). Not re-taught: variable names and the Change / Measure / Keep the same frame (fa1-v21). The agar plan itself is fa2-v03's.
videos.nextHandoff: bio-y11-fa2-v03: the SA:V agar-cube experiment (fa2-v02's existing Next chip)

videos.title: How do you carry out a biology investigation safely and systematically, so every reading and source you record can be used?
videos.mainLearnerQuestion: How do you carry out a biology investigation safely and systematically, so every reading and source you record can be used?
videos.onScreenHeading: How do you collect biology data safely and systematically?

syllabusActions.text: Apply safe work practices and manage risks while conducting a scientific investigation
Construct and manipulate identified materials and technologies to perform scientific investigations
Use equipment appropriately and systematically to collect and record data, information, evidence and findings
Gather data and information from a range of secondary sources

videos.sourceLessonNote: No Working scientifically lesson exists on the site (teaching-app-fix biology/year11 has fa1, fa2 and fa3 only; checked 23 Nov 2026). Contexts come from the Year 11 Biology designs named in entryKnowledge.

placement.rule: Restore-and-pass: the WS video opens on its predecessor's final frame and ends on that same frame (the successor's opening frame), so only the predecessor's Next chip text changes. See bio-y11-gap-fix-status-2026-11-23.md, change C5.

entryKnowledge.idea: A justified plan and risk assessment.
Conditions for photosynthesis (light, carbon dioxide, temperature).

videos.biologyContext: Carrying out ws-v02's potato-cylinder osmosis plan: tare the balance, blot the same way every time, record raw masses in a table drawn before starting, keep the odd reading and note why; managing the scalpel and spills while working; gathering secondary data on the same question from more than one source and recording each source. Leaves the pondweed conduct to fa2-v07.
videos.openingFrame: Open on bio-y11-fa2-v06's final frame (its Next chip edited to this video's on-screen heading).
videos.startBoundary: Recall the preceding result in one sentence, then start from the main learner question with a concrete biology observation.
videos.stopBoundary: Managing risks while working (not only on paper); assembling and checking apparatus before data (zeroing, calibration, trial run); systematic recording: a raw-data table drawn first, units in headings, consistent decimal places, every reading including odd ones with a note, observations; gathering secondary data from a range of sources and recording where each came from. Not taught: processing (ws-v04), analysis statistics (ws-v05).
videos.nextHandoff: bio-y11-fa2-v07: the pondweed photosynthesis investigation (fa2-v06's existing Next chip)

videos.title: Why must raw readings be converted, organised into the right representation and sourced before they count as evidence?
videos.mainLearnerQuestion: Why must raw readings be converted, organised into the right representation and sourced before they count as evidence?
videos.onScreenHeading: How do raw readings become data you can use and cite?

syllabusActions.text: Select qualitative and quantitative information from texts, diagrams, flow charts, tables, databases, graphs and multimedia resources
Apply quantitative processes to data, including unit conversions
Select and use a range of representations to organise data and information, including graphs, keys, models, diagrams, tables and spreadsheets
Extract data and information from a wide range of sources and acknowledge these sources using an accepted referencing style
Describe the Cultural Knowledges and observations of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples and examine how these contribute to the development of scientific knowledge

entryKnowledge.idea: Potometer: bubble distance ÷ time gives the rate of water uptake (mm/min).
Not yet watched at this point; G4-05 is handled with a general forward-looking example and recalled again in ws-v07.

videos.biologyContext: Potometer readings converted from mm/min to µL/min with the tube's bore (πr² × distance); choosing a table, line graph or bar chart; a dichotomous key as a representation; referencing a source in one accepted style; how observations by Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples contribute to scientific knowledge, with a general example (knowledge holders' observations of where and when animals occur helping surveys find threatened species), no names (owner rule). Seasonal indicators and megafauna evidence are left to fa3-v16 and fa3-v05.
videos.openingFrame: Open on bio-y11-fa2-v14's final frame (its Next chip edited to this video's on-screen heading).
videos.startBoundary: Recall the preceding result in one sentence, then start from the main learner question with a concrete biology observation.
videos.stopBoundary: Selecting the information a question needs from a table, graph or text; unit conversions with working (mm to µL, mm to µm, per minute to per hour); choosing a representation by data type (continuous: line graph; categories: bar chart; identification: a key); acknowledging every source in one accepted style (author, year, title, publisher or URL, date accessed); Cultural Knowledges described in general terms with their contribution (long-term observation, seasonal records) and the attribution principle. No named communities (owner rule, 18 Nov 2026).

videos.title: How do repeated biology measurements become a result you can trust, and how sure can you be about it?
videos.mainLearnerQuestion: How do repeated biology measurements become a result you can trust, and how sure can you be about it?
videos.onScreenHeading: How sure can you be about a result?

syllabusActions.text: Describe qualitative and quantitative relationships between variables
Explain patterns and trends, including inconsistencies in data and information
Assess error, uncertainty and limitations in data and include calculations of percentage error, range, mean and standard deviation
Assess the validity, reliability, accuracy and precision of data and information
Interpret data and information to identify outliers, make predictions, explain results and draw conclusions
Evaluate data and information to suggest improvements or further investigations

videos.sourceLessonNote: No Working scientifically lesson exists on the site (teaching-app-fix biology/year11 has fa1, fa2 and fa3 only; checked 23 Nov 2026). Contexts come from the Year 11 Biology designs named in entryKnowledge.

entryKnowledge.idea: Bead mark-release-recapture model: N = M × C ÷ R; repeats 250, 288, 223; the beads can be counted (260).
Mean of three trials; an anomaly; reliability and validity.

videos.biologyContext: The bead model's known true count (260) gives a real percentage error; the three repeats and added class repeats give mean, range and standard deviation; one class value of 520 (a counting slip) is the outlier; accuracy against precision shown with marks that wash off (precise but biased).
videos.openingFrame: Open on bio-y11-fa3-v28's final frame (its Next chip edited to this video's on-screen heading).
videos.startBoundary: Recall the preceding result in one sentence, then start from the main learner question with a concrete biology observation.
videos.stopBoundary: Describing relationships qualitatively and quantitatively; patterns, trends and inconsistencies; percentage error = |experimental − accepted| ÷ accepted × 100; range; mean; standard deviation as the typical distance of readings from the mean (calculator method shown, formula on screen); identifying an outlier and deciding with a stated reason whether to exclude it; validity, reliability, accuracy and precision distinguished on one picture; suggesting improvements and further investigations. Before fa3-v32, which can then recall precision and spread.
videos.nextHandoff: bio-y11-fa3-v29: relationships between organisms (fa3-v28's existing Next chip)

videos.title: How can a biology model solve a real problem, and why is current scientific knowledge both contestable and testable?
videos.mainLearnerQuestion: How can a biology model solve a real problem, and why is current scientific knowledge both contestable and testable?
videos.onScreenHeading: Why is biology knowledge both contestable and testable?

syllabusActions.text: Apply scientific principles to address real-world applications and problems
Use modelling and cause-and-effect relationships, including mathematical examples, to make predictions, explain phenomena and solve problems
Evaluate and modify a scientific investigation in response to new evidence
Explain why current scientific knowledge is both contestable and testable by further inquiry

entryKnowledge.idea: Mark-release-recapture as a model; carrying capacity.
Biogeography as evidence for evolution (southern beech on several southern continents).

videos.biologyContext: Applying the mark-release-recapture model to a real management problem (a feral predator estimate) and modifying the plan when marks are lost; a contested explanation tested by new methods: southern beech distribution, Gondwana separation against later dispersal, tested by molecular dating.
videos.openingFrame: Open on bio-y11-fa3-v32's final frame (its Next chip edited to this video's on-screen heading).

videos.stopBoundary: Applying principles to a real-world problem; using a model with cause and effect, including a calculation, to predict; evaluating and modifying an investigation in response to new evidence; current knowledge is contestable (open to challenge with evidence) and testable (makes predictions new evidence could contradict), with one biology case. Not taught: peer review (ws-v07).

syllabusActions.text: Construct evidence-based arguments and recognise the role of peer review in the evaluation of scientific practices, solutions or conclusions
Select and use appropriate digital, visual, written and oral media to convey scientific arguments
Apply appropriate scientific notations, language and nomenclature
Use evidence and correct scientific language and terminology to address a specific audience and purpose in a variety of contexts

entryKnowledge.idea: Validity, reliability and accuracy of sampling data.

videos.biologyContext: A quadrat survey conclusion written as claim, evidence, reasoning; peer review with a published case that overturned a consensus (bacteria and stomach ulcers, 1980s); binomial names in italics, SI units, significant figures; the same finding written for a report and for a community noticeboard.
